title: Rebuilding Incumbents for AI Beats Investing in Startups
dek: AI's impact on the economy is uneven: restaurants and golf courses are untouched, but incumbents with brands, licenses and network effects can become market leaders once they are re-engineered.
why: Medium information density, but it offers a counterintuitive investment framework: don't fund startups, buy incumbents and rebuild the organization with an engineering team. Suited to anyone watching AI deployment and M&A.
who: Investors and founders focused on AI deployment, M&A and incumbent transformation, especially those who want to understand the logic of "don't fund startups, buy the leaders."
skip: The founder-reflection segment from 34:45 to 36:08, which is low density.

points.h: AI's impact on the economy is uneven
points.body: Michael Lee argues AI will not change every industry evenly. Restaurants and golf courses are industries AI will never touch; in industries like writing code, startups win — he notes that Conviction and Sequence were going to buy a coding-outsourcing company, which sounds like a terrible idea, but you would put your money into Cognition or Anthropic. What actually excites him is the third category: incumbents that own brands, scale, network effects or regulatory barriers. If you can graft state-of-the-art technology and engineering onto them, you have a shot at turning them into market leaders. Sequence's entire model is built on this judgment.

Michael explains why incumbents cannot complete the AI transition themselves with the idea that "every company has a celebrity." Blackstone's celebrity is the investor, which is how it unites the world's largest capital allocators; but in a world that believes alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need the engineer to be the celebrity who commands respect. Palantir is essentially a collection of world-class engineers wrapped in a shell and sold to organizations that cannot hire such people. If you cannot hire them yourself, going to service providers like Accenture or McKinsey does not work either — their incentive is to keep you paying, and their path is incrementalism. Buying software is worse: software sells the workflows that already exist today, whereas AI requires redesigning a human assembly line that does not exist yet.

points.h: A bank is the perfect cold-start testbed
points.body: When Sequence was founded it faced a cold-start problem: no money means no deals, no deals means no engineers, and no engineers means nobody gives you money. They decided to land one customer first to prove themselves. Through a friend's introduction they met a family bank in Georgia, entered as a service provider last August, and worked on key workflows for several months. The bank then asked whether they wanted to become a permanent partner, which became Sequence's first investment, closing in March this year, with approvals from the Federal Reserve and the OCC along the way. Michael says being regulated is actually a feature, not a bug, for a bank: operations are clearly defined and data hygiene is excellent, which makes it very well suited to agents.

points.h: Insurance brokerage is the archetypal incumbent
points.body: Sequence spent a lot of time studying insurance brokerage. In this industry more than $2 trillion in premiums flows to insurers each year, brokers do not charge clients — insurers pay them — customer retention runs as high as 90%, and brokers find it very hard to compete on price. These traits make it extremely difficult for startups to break in. Michael says insurers' underwriting business has barely been profitable throughout history, with profits coming mainly from investing, so they are motivated to accumulate assets, which in turn makes brokers very powerful. Baldwin meets all of Sequence's criteria: a huge market, an incumbent insulated from startup risk, and a management team already pushing technology into deployment.

points.h: Atlas abstracts out 80% of the commonality for reuse
points.body: Atlas is the platform Sequence built inside the bank, and they expect it to generalize across all industries. That judgment comes from an observation: if you break a business down into atomic units, 80% is highly homogeneous and 20% is vertical-specific. Atlas has four layers. The first is the data ontology, defining in code how the organization and the business operate so models can understand the company. The second is the agent builder, which builds high-performance agents on top of the underlying data. The third is called lattice, the orchestration mechanism that actually wires agents into workflows. The top layer is called artifacts, the application-building layer. Michael says all the core infrastructure they built in the bank can be reused for Baldwin and for any future company.

Michael concedes that large PE firms have the motivation, resources and capability to do AI transformation, but he thinks they face several structural limits. The first is talent: a typical PE firm is designed to make the investor the celebrity, whereas world-class engineers want to be part of the decisions, and it is very rare for a 25-year-old engineer at a large buyout firm to have a say in investment decisions. The second is time horizon: under a fund structure you are usually thinking about how to package and sell in three years, a completely different formula from the long-term commitment a technology transformation requires. The third is deal cadence: Sequence does one deal a year, has no deployment cadence, and no LP pushing them because they did not invest enough this year. Michael says he wants to hold Sequence equity for life.

points.h: The hard numbers on the bank transformation
points.body: From the March investment to the time of recording, about 6 months, Sequence built a system in the bank that can take on all consumer lending in the organization. Average consumer loan underwriting volume fell 94% versus March. Commercial loan underwriting came online in recent months, and average loan processing time dropped from 30 days to 11 days. Michael says this lets the bank take on far more loan volume with the same headcount. In this year's second quarter, the bank's loan volume doubled versus the first quarter. Historically the bank had turned customers away because of limited middle- and back-office bandwidth; now, with underwriting standards completely unchanged, the bank handled all the loan volume, and the underwriting team is smaller than before the investment — because one person retired and one moved to the front office.

points.h: Betting on people beats betting on ideas
points.body: Michael says that if he were redesigning how to do PE today, he would only look for exceptional people solving complex problems in huge markets. From his experience at Sequence he learned that ideas are cheap, execution is very hard, and truly exceptional people always find a way to get things done — because they bring in people who cover their weaknesses, or they are persistent enough to find backers to do the thing everyone thinks is crazy. Everything else, whether it is the best idea you have ever seen or the hottest breakthrough of the moment, is just an important signal, but this business today is ultimately about people, especially at the early stage.
